> **What this case shows** — SPM tests *whether two groups of curves differ*;
> **functional regression** models a curve as a *function of a covariate*, giving
> a **coefficient curve** — how, and *where along the movement*, the waveform
> changes per unit predictor. On 42 adults walking at 8 treadmill speeds, the
> ecosystem recovers the established speed-dependence of the knee: the fitted
> **speed-coefficient curve** is significant (curve-wide permutation **p =
> 0.0005**), **positive**, and peaks at **65% of the gait cycle** — the
> swing-flexion peak — at **+3.34° per speed level** (faster walking = more knee
> flexion), with a second positive lobe at the loading-response flexion (~15%).
> Pooled peak knee flexion rises with speed (**r = 0.63**). **What reproduces** —
> exactly the speed-modulation gait biomechanics describes, with a method that
> localises *where* in the cycle speed acts. **How to read it** — left, one
> subject's knee angle fanning open with speed; centre, the speed-coefficient
> curve (where speed matters); right, peak flexion rising with speed.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to relate a *waveform* to a *scalar* covariate, fit a pointwise
linear model across the cycle and read the **coefficient curve** with its
curve-wide (family-wise) permutation p-value — the functional analogue of a
regression slope.
**Way of thinking** — a coefficient *curve* answers "*where* along the movement
does the predictor act?", which a single scalar (e.g. peak flexion) cannot; and
remove each subject's mean first so the coefficient is the **within-subject**
effect, not a between-subject artefact.
**Ecosystem usage** — `functionalRegression()` (PhysioAnalysis) on a curves ×
covariate design; pair with `scalarOnFunctionRegression()` for the reverse
direction.
:::

## Proposition

On real gait kinematics, function-on-scalar regression recovers the established
speed-dependence of the knee waveform — a significant (p = 0.0005), positive
speed-coefficient curve peaking at the swing-flexion (65% cycle, +3.34°/level),
with peak knee flexion rising with speed (r = 0.63).

## Question & goal

**The question is where, not just whether.** It is textbook that people flex the
knee more as they walk faster — but *where in the gait cycle* does speed act, and
how much? A scalar summary (peak flexion) throws away the shape. The WBDS dataset
was built as *reference gait kinematics* across a speed sweep precisely so these
speed–waveform relationships can be modelled. We ask: does a function-on-scalar
regression, on these real angles, recover the speed-dependence and localise it?

## Challenge & approach

We take the sagittal knee angle (`RKneeAngleZ`) over the gait cycle for 42 adults
at 8 treadmill speeds, remove each subject's across-speed mean (so the coefficient
is the within-subject speed effect, uncontaminated by between-subject offsets),
and fit `functionalRegression()` of the knee curve on the (centred, ordinal) speed
level. The coefficient curve is tested curve-wide by permutation.

## Data

**WBDS** (Fukuchi et al. 2018) — 42 adults, 3D motion capture, sagittal knee angle
over the gait cycle at 8 treadmill speeds (328 subject-speed curves). Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![One subject's knee angle by speed (left; fast in yellow reaches a higher swing
peak), the fitted speed-coefficient curve (centre; positive where speed increases
flexion) and peak knee flexion versus speed (right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the centre panel is the recipe's product — the coefficient
curve peaks at **65%** (swing-flexion) and again near **15%** (loading response),
the two moments where speed most opens the knee, and dips toward zero through
mid-stance. The whole curve is significant by a family-wise permutation test.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| speed coefficient peak location | **65% cycle** (swing) |
| speed coefficient at peak | **+3.34°** per speed level |
| curve-wide permutation p | **0.0005** |
| peak-flexion vs speed correlation | **r = 0.63** |
| subject-speed curves | **328** (42 subjects × 8 speeds) |

## Conclusion

Function-on-scalar regression recovers, on real gait, exactly the speed-dependence
of the knee the literature describes — and pins it to the swing-flexion and
loading-response moments. The transferable takeaway: **when a waveform depends on
a covariate, fit a coefficient *curve*, not a scalar — it tells you *where* the
covariate acts — and remove subject means first so the effect is within-subject.**

## Open questions

- Modelling speed in **m/s** (not an ordinal level) would make the coefficient
  read as degrees per m/s and compare across labs; that needs the WBDS per-subject
  speed table. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| joint-angle curves from markers | `calculateJointAngles()` | PhysioMoCap |
| function-on-scalar (coefficient curve + p) | `functionalRegression()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| scalar-from-curve (reverse) | `scalarOnFunctionRegression()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| multilevel (strides in subjects) | `functionalMixedModel()` | PhysioAnalysis |

**Choosing the parameters:** pass one row per curve and the matching covariate,
remove nuisance means (here each subject's) first, use enough permutations
(≥1000) for a stable curve-wide p, and read the **coefficient curve** — its sign
says the direction, its shape says *where* the covariate acts.

```r
library(PhysioAnalysis)
fit <- functionalRegression(knee_curves, speed, n_perm = 2000)
fit$coefficients["x1", ]   # the speed coefficient CURVE (deg per unit speed)
fit$p_global["x1"]         # curve-wide (family-wise) significance
```
